q39_quota_ledger.ask: An agent estate meters dollars per API call, but its BINDING currency is a provider rolling-window quota: request capacity inside a 5-hour sliding window per account. Two banked failure modes: (a) a 50-request parallel burst on one account triggered a storm of HTTP 429 responses that crashed tethered sessions; (b) two bursts 4 hours apart succeed while the same two bursts 30 minutes apart fail, and nothing predicts which. The disease: the metered currency (dollars) is not the binding currency (the window), and the window has no ledger. Design the WINDOW METER: 1) the data structure(s) tracking rolling-window consumption exactly enough to predict whether a proposed burst of N requests fits the remaining window, with memory bounds; 2) the update path on every dispatch and every 429 response, including how a quota 429 is distinguished from a hard error; 3) the prediction API the dispatcher calls before fanning out: signature, semantics, and behavior under uncertainty; 4) the recovery policy when the prediction was wrong (mid-burst 429s); 5) a falsifier test: two burst schedules the ledger predicts hold vs fail, testable without wall-clock waiting. Constraints: one process plus an append-only jsonl log is the persistence; no external services. Close by naming the ONE design decision most likely wrong and how your falsifier catches it.

q03_frame_mac.ask: A game server authenticates clients with an SRP6 handshake (shared key K established, 256-bit group, SHA1). After the handshake, all frames are line-JSON over raw TCP with no MAC and no TLS: any on-path party can flip a byte of a move frame and the server attributes the forged move to the authenticated identity. Design post-auth frame integrity: 1) the exact MAC construction over each frame (what is covered, key derivation from K, per-frame nonce/counter and why replay is impossible); 2) the migration path for already-shipped clients (versioning, fallback, kill date); 3) the failure behavior on a bad MAC (drop, disconnect, receipt row?); 4) the interplay with a later TLS transition (does the MAC survive, retire, or double-cover?); 5) a falsifier test: complete one real handshake, flip one byte of the next frame, assert rejection with the specific error. Close with the one decision most likely wrong and its catching test.

q02_hydrology_family.ask: Two fixed-point water engines (Python and GDScript) implement the same laws and once diverged silently on 29/100 seeded boards (a parity harness exists: generator families mountain, gated_siblings, economy, fracture_loop, random; boards are nodes with volume/cross_section, ticked 40+ ticks, state hashed per tick, any hash mismatch = divergence). Known blind spot: no family varies cross_section or grade-sensitive volumes, so gradient-head arithmetic (head_scale 256 graded-head routing) is untested in both directions. Design the MISSING generator family: 1) the exact board-space it samples (cross_section values incl. 1, 7, 1000, milli-depth edges; topology shapes that stress head routing); 2) why each choice targets a DIFFERENT arithmetic path in the engine (name the operation class: fixed-point multiply, divide, saturating add, ordering); 3) the seed discipline so a divergence found is reproducible byte-exact; 4) the acceptance predicate (what counts as caught); 5) the falsifier: the minimal single board that would have caught a known past divergence (spring volume -1 vs 0, terrace 1 vs 0). Close with the one choice most likely wrong and its catching test.

r1_route_coldstart.source: AD4_GPS_SPEC AMENDMENT 5 + D2_GPS_ROUTES (route open design question)
r1_route_coldstart.ask: A model router routes task shapes to model families using a capability table: per (family, shape) pass_rate over a calibration window of m=50 verdicts; qualification and routing are gated on n >= m; while n < m the router is in cold start: exploration only, forced probes, receipts marked calibration_state: unverified, confidence never climbs. Open design question: the cold-start FORCED-PROBE ALLOCATION. There are 8 families and 5 task shapes = 40 cells x 50 verdicts = 2000 paid verdicts to fill the table; that budget will never exist. Design the allocation policy: 1) how the next forced probe (family, shape) is chosen while n < m (name the exact rule: round-robin, uncertainty-first, regret-bound, priors from duel wins, something else); 2) how per-shape demand weights real traffic so hot shapes calibrate first; 3) when a family is retired from a shape early (thresholds, evidence rule); 4) how the policy degrades when only 10 percent of the fill budget ever materializes; 5) the falsifier: two probe sequences where policy A reaches a routable state strictly cheaper than policy B, with the cost model stated. Close with the one choice most likely wrong and its catching test.

q26_load_region.ask: A room-based game server (one authoritative world tick per room, blocking TCP door plus an asyncio websocket door, snapshot broadcast per tick) has only ever been tested with a handful of localhost connections. Design the load bench that first contacts the truth: 1) the bench topology (process count, peers per process, think-time model, verb mix incl. illegal verbs) and why each knob targets a distinct server path (room pump, broadcast fan-out, store writes); 2) the metrics with units and collection points (tick time distribution, broadcast backlog, memory, divergent disconnects); 3) the ladder of plateaus (50 peers, 500 peers) with stop conditions and the visible-degradation law (never fail silently); 4) how the bench detects head-of-line blocking across the two transports; 5) the falsifier: one run whose numbers would prove the server CANNOT hold 50 strangers, stated before the run. Close with the one decision most likely wrong and its catching test.

q14_flock_parity.ask: One flocking simulation exists in four ports claimed from one law set: GDScript, Luau, JavaScript, and Python/numpy. No harness has ever fed all ports the same seeded frame and compared positions after N ticks. Design that harness: 1) the shared input format (one seeded frame: agents, radii (school/flee/trail), constants) and the canonical output hash (float quantization rule, agent ordering) so ports with different float stacks compare honestly; 2) the driver per port (headless entry point, stdin/stdout contract) and how the Luau and JS ports run without a game host; 3) the divergence report (first differing tick, first differing agent, delta magnitude, not just a boolean); 4) the drift ledger across runs; 5) the falsifier: the seeded frame most likely to split the ports (boundary condition: agent exactly at flee radius) and the predicate that catches it. Close with the one decision most likely wrong and its catching test.
